title: Coils in the 120-cell
statement: The 120-cell is the regular 4-dimensional polytope with 600 vertices; its graph is 4-regular with girth 5. Its vertices correspond to the 600 tetrahedral cells of the 600-cell, two vertices being adjacent when their cells share a triangle. A coil (coil-in-the-box) is an induced cycle: a cycle in the graph with no edge between two of its vertices other than the cycle's own edges. How long can a coil in the 120-cell be? Best known: 202 vertices (ours); every coil has at most 400.
submission: Text file: one line 'a b c d' per vertex of the coil, in the order of the cycle, each vertex written as its tetrahedral cell of the 600-cell (four vertex numbers 0..119, numbered as in checkers/orig_codes.py).
score: the number of vertices of the coil (larger is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: randomised greedy growth of induced paths that prefers the step blocking the fewest free vertices, recording every closing induced cycle, many restarts (tools/src/coil.c)

context: Snake-in-the-box codes (Kautz 1958) are long induced paths and cycles in the hypercube: read as codes, consecutive words differ in one coordinate and any two other words in at least two, so a single error is detected; exact values are known only up to dimension 8, and records in higher dimensions are still being improved (2026). The question makes sense in any graph, and the 120-cell, the four-dimensional analogue of the dodecahedron, is a natural one: sparse (degree 4), with girth 5 and a symmetry group of order 14,400. A coil there is a closed walk through its vertices in which no two walk vertices are neighbours unless consecutive. Our searches find coils through a third of the 600 vertices. Counting gives the bound 400: each coil vertex has two neighbours off the coil, and each of the other 600 - c vertices has at most four neighbours, so 2c <= 4(600 - c). The gap between our coils and 400, and the longest induced path (snake), are open.
references: W. H. Kautz, Unit-distance error-checking codes, IRE Trans. Electronic Computers EC-7 (1958) 179-180
H. S. M. Coxeter, Regular Polytopes, 3rd ed., Dover (1973)
P. R. J. Ostergard, V. H. Pettersson, Exhaustive search for snake-in-the-box codes, Graphs Combin. 31 (2015) 1019-1028
A census of new snake-in-the-box records, arXiv:2607.15270 (2026)

novelty.verdict: new question for this graph: snake-in-the-box and coil-in-the-box are studied for hypercubes and other cube-like graphs; nothing was found on induced cycles or paths of the 120-cell.
closest: Snake-in-the-box and coil-in-the-box in the hypercube (Kautz 1958; exhaustive values to dimension 8; records still improved in 2026): the same question in another graph.
Snakes in Fibonacci cubes (in the OEIS; dropped by us) and our problem cell600-forest (largest induced forest of the 600-cell): other induced-subgraph questions.
novelty.benchmark: no snake-in-the-box family in the benchmark

first_values.note: tools/src/coil.c with 30 s and 400 s of search; the certificate lists the cells of the 600-cell.

baseline.text: 202 vertices, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: the coil in `refs/cell120-coil.txt`. Upper bound 400 (counting edges between the coil and the rest).

bound.source: each of the c coil vertices has 2 neighbours off the coil and each of the other 600 - c vertices at most 4, so 2c <= 4(600 - c)
